(ORAL)
1. Vide this judgment, I propose to dispose off the appeal filed against the order of conviction dated 02.08.2016 and order on sentence dated 06.08.2016, passed by Ld. ACMMII, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi.
2. The brief facts of the case as per record are that accused was the vendorcumproprietor of M/s Priya Tea Stall, Kiosk No.29, Dr. Rajender Prasad Road, New Delhi01.

On 19.07.2004, Food Inspector Sh. Jeet Ram alongwith Field Assistant Sh. Pratap Raj and SDM (LHA) Sh. S.K. Sachdeva visited the said stall and 750 grams of Vanaspati (ready for use) stored in an open tin bearing no label declaration was taken.
The said sample was divided into three parts and packed as per Rules.

1
Panchanama was prepared.
One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst.

As per the report of Analyst, sample was not conforming to the standards because it gave negative Baudouin test on mixing of groundnut oil in the ratio 20:80 in terms of standard A.19 Appendix B to the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.

It would be pertinent to note at this stage itself that the Baudouin test is recommended by (x) of the Standards recommended under A.19 of Appendix B to the PFA Rules for detecting the refined sesame (til) oil in the Vanaspati.

The relevant portion of the Schedule Standard A.19 is reproduced hereinbelow for ease of reference:
A.19...
(x) It shall contain raw or refined sesame (til) oil in sufficient quantity so that when the vanaspati is mixed with refined groundnut oil in the proportion of 20:80, the colour produced by the Baudouin test shall not be lighter than 2.0 red unit in a 1cm.
cell on a Lovibond scale;

3. The report of the PA reads as follows:
1. BT (vanaspati mixed with refined groundnut oil in the proportion of 20:80)
Result Negative. Standard: Not less than 2.0 red units.
4.

Similarly, report of the CFL reads as follows:
6. Test for -do- Negative Shall be a) Baudouin on positive Red Dilution 20:80 units 2.0 on sample : Ref. Lovibond Groundnut Oil Tintometer Scale in 1 cm b) Agremone oil -do- Negative cell 5.

Therefore, from the aforesaid, it is evident that the PA and CFL both tested the sample for presence of sesame oil and concluded that the same was not detected in consonance with the standard and method prescribed.
6. As the sample had failed to pass the analysis, prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint with the court.
Accused was summoned for facing trial.

7. Charge was framed against the accused under Section 2 (ia)
(a) & (m) of PFA Act; punishable under Section 16 (1) (a) read with Section 7 of the Act of 1954 in these facts and circumstances.

8. After trial, vide judgment dated 02.08.2016, accused was convicted for offence under Section 7/16 (1) (a) of PFA Act and vide order dated 06.08.2016, accused was sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one year and fine of Rs.40,000/ and in default of payment of fine SI Rajesh Gupta vs . 9. In order to prove its case, the prosecution examined following witnesses:
PW1 SDM/LHA S.K. Sachdeva PW2 FI Jeet Ram PW3 FA Pratap Raj 10.

Prosecution exhibited the following documents:
Ex.PW1/A Vendor receipt Ex.PW1/B Notice in Form VI Ex.PW1/C Panchnama Ex.PW1/D Photocopy of NDMC fine receipt Ex.PW1/E Two counterparts of sample alongwith two copies of  Form VII Ex.PW1/F Intimation regarding one counterpart deposited with PA Ex.PW1/G PA report Ex.PW1/H Letter to STO Ward no.3 Ex.PW1/J Consent for prosecution Ex.PW1/K Complaint Ex.PW2/A Intimation letter Ex.PW2/B
Postal registration receipt copy 11.
In his defence, the accused did not lead any evidence.

In his Statement under Section 313 Cr.PC,
the accused denied all allegations and claimed that he was falsely implicated in the present case.
12. Arguments heard.
Record perused.
13. In the present case, the Public Analyst report could not detect the presence of sesame oil in the sample lifted from the premises of the appellant.
This aspect is noted in para 12 of the Trial Court's judgment.
14. To my mind, the entire dispute, at this stage, is on the aspect whether the Baudouin test can be considered as a reliable test for detecting adulteration in Vanaspati.

Counsel for appellant has restricted his arguments to the aspect that Baudouin test is not an infallible test and stands discredited in view of the decisions of the Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court in Municipal Committee Amritsar Vs. Mehar Singh, Crl. Appeal No. 207/1969 decided on 18.05.1972; Sohan Lal Vs. The State of Punjab, PFA 1983 (I) 48, following the aforesaid decision and State Vs. Mahavir Prashad, 2005 (1) C.C. Cases (HC) 397 of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi.

I have noticed that both the decision in Mehar Singh (Supra) and Mahavir Prashad (Supra) were relied upon before the Ld. MM, who chose to distinguish the said judgments on the ground that no evidence was led by the accused to show that the Til Oil was from the Mediterranean region.
Further, that accused had not taken any such defence nor examined any chemical expert.
The said aspect is relevant as decision in Municipal Committee Amritsar (Supra) and Mahavir Prashad (Supra) takes note of the fact that Mediterranean Oil cannot be detected by Baudouin test.
In fact, it seems that the same is also applicable to Til obtained from Tripura.
The decision of Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court categorically noted that nothing was shown to indicate that the Mediterranean seeds were not available in India.

Ld. MM, on the other hand, reversed this onus in the present case, on the accused, despite the fact that the decision of the Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court and also the one passed by the Delhi High Court, approving the ruling of the Hon'ble Punjab and Haryana High Court were before him.
In fact, the relevant portion of both the decisions is reproduced as follows:

Municipal Committee Amritsar (Supra):
Report Exhibit P. F. of the Public Analyst read with his statement recorded on 24th April 1972, points out that he (Public Analyst) carried out four tests and found that sample of the Vanaspati satisfied three out of the aforesaid four tests.

In other words,
it was found to fulfil the standards mentioned at (v), (vi) and (viii), stated under rule A. 19 reproduced above.

He (Public Analyst), however found that the sample of Vanaspati did not fulfil the standard laid in (x) of rule A19, because the analysis,
carried out by him, revealed that it did not contain any sesame (til) oil.
According to the said standard, prescribed in (x) of rule A19, the sample of Vanaspati should have contained raw or refined sesame ( oil not less than 5 per cent by weight.
The procedure or method by which sesame (til) oil can be detected in the Vanaspati is called Baudouin tests.

The said test means that, when sesame oil is shaken with concentrated hydrochloric acid and then made to react with a solution of furfural in alcohol, it gives red colour (vide page 55 of 'The Vanaspati Industry' by Gopal S.
Harttiangdi, Fin Edition 1958.

Shri Ravinder Nath Beri, Public Analyst admits, in his statement recorded on 24th April, 1972, that there are certain varieties of sesame til oil imported from the Mediterranean region when added to the Vanaspati in the ratio, as stated in (x) of rule A19, it would not, when the Vanaspati is subjected to Baudouin test, give red colour.

There is nothing on the record to show that no sesame (til) oil, imported from the Mediterranean region is available in India Therefore, the possibility, as contended by the learned counsel for the respondent, that the Vanaspati possessed by the respondent, could contain sesame (til) imported from the Mediterranean region, to the extent of 5 per cent or more by weight and, therefore, it did not respond to the Baudouin test, cannot be excluded.

In that view of the matter,
the Vanaspati, possessed by the respondent, from which the sample had been taken cannot be declared, with certainty, to be adulterated.

Since the sesame (til) oil imported from the Mediterranean region does not respond to the Baudouin test, the same (Baudouin test) cannot be said to be sure test for finding that the Vanaspati does not contain sesame (til) Oil to the extent of 5 per cent, by weight.

Rajesh Gupta vs . Delhi Administration on 28 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/103857142/
4 ...
The main purpose of adding sesame (til) oil to Vanaspati, as admitted by Shri Ravinder Nath Beri.
Public Analyst, in his statement recorded on 24th April 1972, is to detect ad alteration of pure ghee with Vanaspati.
He further admits in his aforesaid statement that the absence of sesame (til) oil in the Vanaspati does not affect its nutritive value.

Therefore, it cannot be said that any colouring matter, other than the one prescribed in respect thereof, had been added to the Vanaspati in question or that its quality or purity had fallen below the prescribed standard.

I, therefore, find force in the contention of the learned counsel for the respondent that, in the circumstances of the case and on the material present on the record, it cannot be held, much less safely, that the Vanaspati, possessed by the respondent, was adulterated.
In that view of the matter, the acquittal of the respondent cannot be interfered with and, therefore, the appeal must fail.

Mahavir Prashad (Supra):
3. The trial court basing its opinion on a judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in MCD Vs/ Mehar Singh [1972 FAC 603] has returned a finding that the vanaspati oil which contained til oil imported from a Mediterranean region did not respond to the baudouin test.

4. With the assistance of the learned counsel for the State, I have gone through the record of the case and find that the opinion of the public analyst was based on the baudouin test and in that view of the matter, the learned Magistrate was perfectly right in not relying upon the test.
Nothing has been shown to me to hold a contrary view or to show that the judgment under challenge is perverse.
In that view of the matter, I find no ground to interfere with the wellreasoned judgment of the trial court.
Crl. A. 211/1984 is accordingly dismissed.

17. Considering the categorical view taken by the Delhi High Court that the Magistrate was not wrong in concluding that the Baudouin test was not infallible, as also, that the Magistrate did no mistake in not relying upon the Baudouin test to conclude adulteration, I am of the view that the Ld.
Trial Court fell at error.

The Ld. MM could not have taken the finding given by the Hon'ble Punjab &
Haryana High Court and the finding given by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court on the reliability of Baudouin test as restricted to those cases only.

18. In my view, even though, the judgment is in personum, the legal principle that can be deducted from the said case that Baudouin test is not infallible test and it cannot detect the presence of all kinds of Til Oil.
Further, the said decision placed the onus on the prosecution to show that the Til seeds from Mediterranean or some other area, which may not be detected by Baudouin test were not available in India.
That being the ratio, which can be culled out from the aforesaid cases, the same will apply on all fours in the present case as well.
Since the analysis and the conclusion are based solely on the Baudouin test, the same conclusion has to be arrived at in the present case.

It would not make any difference whether the Public Analyst was examined or not, as infallibility of the Baudouin test was adjudicated upon by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court and the Hon'ble Punjab &

19. In that view of the matter, the present appellant/convict is entitled to benefit of doubt, on this ground.
20. Appellant/accused is acquitted accordingly.
21. TCR be sent back.
22. Appeal file be consigned to Record Room.
